title: Insular minuscule script
subtitle: The rounded, compressed hand of the early Irish and Northumbrian manuscripts
excerpt: Insular minuscule is the script of the Book of Kells, the Lindisfarne Gospels, and the main corpus of early medieval Irish and Northumbrian manuscripts. It is a compressed, wedge-seriffed hand written with the pen held at a very flat angle. Learning even the basic letterforms gives a reader access to one of the most historically significant scripts in European book production.
sourceNotes: Edward Johnston, Writing and Illuminating and Lettering (1906), chapter on historical scripts: description of insular half-uncial and insular minuscule letterforms from manuscript sources. Johnston drew directly from facsimiles of the Lindisfarne Gospels and the Book of Kells for his analysis of the letter proportions and pen angle.

glossaryTerms.definition: The script developed in the monasteries of Ireland and Northumbria from the sixth to the ninth century, characterised by a compressed round body, a near-flat pen angle (0 to 5 degrees from the writing line), and distinctive wedge-shaped serifs made by pulling the pen upward at the start of ascenders.
A tapered triangular entry stroke that begins the vertical stems in insular minuscule. Made by placing the nib at a near-flat angle, pulling upward slightly, then pulling down into the stem.

In insular minuscule, the nib is held almost parallel to the writing line (0 to 5 degrees from horizontal), unlike the 30 to 45 degree angles used in Foundational or Italic work. This produces very different thick-thin patterns in the letterforms.

content.text: Insular minuscule is one of the most demanding calligraphy scripts to learn. The pen angle differs radically from all other broad-edge hands. The nib is held almost flat to the writing line (the
of 0 to 5 degrees from horizontal). At this angle, horizontal strokes are the thickest parts of letters and vertical stems are the thinnest. This is the opposite of Foundational hand. The
alphabet has a compressed, rounded x-height of 4 to 5 nib widths, with long ascenders and descenders.

items.name: Mitchell Roundhand nib, 3 (medium)
items.notes: Start at Mitchell 3 for a working scale. The flat angle on a wide nib (Mitchell 0 or 1) is difficult to control while also learning the letterforms.

items.name: Iron-gall ink or sumi ink
items.notes: Both flow well at the flat angle. Avoid thick inks: the nib edges need to release ink freely at the near-horizontal position.

items.name: Cartridge paper, 130 gsm
items.notes: Ruled at 5 nib-widths x-height with ascender and descender lines.

content.text: Rule a horizontal line on practice paper. Hold the nib above the line and rotate the pen holder until the top edge of the nib (the back edge) is nearly parallel to the line. Check by drawing a short diagonal: the thickest part of the stroke should be at roughly 5 to 10 degrees from horizontal. This will feel very wrong if Foundational hand is your primary script: the nib angle is nearly upside-down from the position you are used to.

is the signature entry stroke of insular minuscule. Place the nib at the baseline of an ascender at the flat angle. Pull the nib upward and slightly to the right for 3 to 4 mm, forming a thin rising hairline. Then pull sharply downward into the stem stroke. The junction of the hairline and the stem forms the wedge shape. Practice the wedge on its own in a column of twenty repetitions before adding it to letters. Consistency of wedge shape is what makes the script look coherent.

The round letters (a, c, d, e, g, o, p, q) in insular minuscule have a compressed oval body at 4 nib-widths x-height. The upright letters (i, l, n, m, u, h) use the wedge entry at the ascender line, a straight thin vertical stem, and an exit curve at the baseline. Begin with the 'i': wedge serif at the top of the x-height, straight stem down to the baseline, a gentle exit foot. Then add the 'u' (two 'i' stems joined at the top), the 'n' (two 'i' stems with an arch), and the 'o' (a compressed oval made in two strokes).

items.symptom: Thick verticals instead of thin verticals
items.cause: The pen angle has drifted back toward 30 to 45 degrees from its correct near-flat position.
items.fix: Stop and re-set the pen angle deliberately against a ruled line. A rubber band around the pen holder can mark the correct rotation.

items.symptom: The wedge serif looks like a blob
items.cause: The upward hairline pull is too short or too slow, and the ink spreads at the junction.
items.fix: The upward pull needs to be quick and decisive: 3 mm in one smooth move, then an immediate sharp pivot downward. Slow the pivot and the ink pools.
